Shinichi Ono, an archaeologist with [[Kato Academy (Shizuoka Prefecture)]], hypothesized that the shrine was located on a tumulus while conducting site investigations in the 1960s associated with the construction of the [[Tōmei Expressway]]."Ah, the Takaozan Kofun: A Cultural Asset Worth Preserving" Numazu Asahi Newspaper, July 2, 2015, front page. In his 1978 publication "Numazu City History in Pictures," Ono introduced the name "Takaozan Kofun," referencing the Homimi Shrine, and classified the tumulus as a [[square tomb]]. However, when Numazu City registered it as an archaeological site, it was recorded under the local name "Tsubahata Kofun."The specific timing of the registration varies between sections of the 2012 excavation report by the Numazu City Board of Education: the preface states 1982, while p. 10 indicates 1979. Due to these inconsistencies, the year is not specified here. However, "Tsubahata" refers to the area north of the tumulus, while the correct local name of Takaozan Kofun is "Hokuhō."Ono (1978) p. 31, Numazu City Board of Education (2012) preface, p. 10
Despite being registered as an archaeological site, no significant investigations were conducted, and no artifacts associated with the tumulus were identified until the construction of the Numazu South Isshiki Line advanced in the Heisei era (1989–2019). By 2005, land acquisitions in the Kumano Shrine and Takaozan Homimi Shrine area were completed. Both shrines were relocated eastward, and concerns arose about the tumulus's existence under Takaozan Homimi Shrine. Consequently, test excavations commenced in 2005, identifying ditch structures and [[haji earthenware]], suggesting the possibility of a square tomb.Numazu City Board of Education (2012) p. 10
From 2007 to 2009, a second round of excavations and a full-scale investigation were conducted, leading to the conclusion that the site was a zenpō-kōhō-fun constructed during the 3rd century, similar to the [[Kōbōzan Kofun]] in [[Matsumoto City]], [[Nagano Prefecture]]. In 2011, the name "Takaozan Kofun," first proposed by Ono, was officially adopted.Numazu City Board of Education (2012) preface, pp. 10–14, Takizawa (2013) p. 5
In 2014, further investigations were conducted to confirm the tumulus's construction date and evaluate the possibility of additional burial facilities.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/pr/interview/pdf/201408_3.pdf Numazu City, 2014, "Results of Additional Excavations at Takaozan Kofun" (PDF file)] Accessed July 6, 2017.
== Location and Environment of the Kofun == [[File:Ashitaka Volcano Relief Map, SRTM-1 and Takaozan kofun.jpg|thumb|300px|Relief map of Mount Ashitaka and surrounding areas. The red circle marks Takaozan Kofun's location, while the southeast area shaded white represents the former Ukishima Marsh.]] Takaozan Kofun is situated at the terminus of a ridge

[[Takaosan Kofun]]{{Expand Japanese}} {{Otheruses||Kofun on Mount Takao in Kashiwara City, Osaka Prefecture (Takaozan Site)|Takaozan (Osaka Prefecture)}} {{Japanese burial mounds |name = Takaozan Kofun |image = [[File:Takaosan-kofun (Numazu) zenkei.JPG|280px]]Full view of the tumulus (foreground left: front section, background right: rear section)(as of June 2015) |location = [[Higashikumando]], [[Numazu City]], [[Shizuoka Prefecture]] |latitude = 35|latitude_min = 7|latitude_sec = 22.73 |longitude =138|longitude_min = 51|longitude_sec = 40.22 |ISO = JP-22 |shape = [[Zenpō-kōhō-fun]] |dimensions = Tumulus length: 62mHeight: 4.7m (estimated at approximately 5m) |burial_facility = [[Wooden coffin]] direct burial |construction_date = Around the year [[250]] |buried_person = |grave_goods = Bronze mirror (animal belt mirror of the embossed style from the Shangfang Workshop) 1 piece, magatama 1 piece, spear 1 piece, 32 iron arrowheads, 1 spearhead-plane, and a large amount of earthenware from the tumulus and the surrounding ditch. |cultural_property_designation = [[Historic Site]] designated by the national government ("Takaozan Kofun") |notable_features = |map = Japan Shizuoka |icon = Zenpō-kōhō-fun - South }} {{osm box|n|4735442868}}
'''Takaozan Kofun''' (Takaozan burial mound) is a [[kofun]] located in [[Higashikumando]] ("East Kumando"), [[Numazu City]], [[Shizuoka Prefecture]]. It has the form of a [[Zenpō-kōhō-fun]] (keyhole-shaped mound with a rectangular rear and trapezoidal front)Numazu City Board of Education (2012) summary report. It has been designated as a [[Historic Site]] by the national government.[https://www.bunka.go.jp/koho_hodo_oshirase/hodohappyo/94070501.html Cultural Council's Recommendation (Designation of Historic Sites, Places of Scenic Beauty, and Natural Monuments)] (Agency for Cultural Affairs press release, June 24, 2024).Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology, Notification No. 142, October 11, 2024.
The Numazu City Board of Education estimates its construction to have been around the year [[250]], during the early [[Kofun period]] (the period of the [[Yamatai Kingdom]]), making it one of the oldest and largest kofun in Eastern Japan from the early appearance of such burial mounds.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/profile/bunkazai/kofun/takaosan.htm Numazu City, 2024, "Takaozan Kofun"] Accessed October 20, 2024. The [[Japanese Archaeological Association]] has evaluated it as an extremely important site for understanding the process of forming the early statehood marked by the kofun culture.[http://archaeology.jp/maibun/nikokyo2015-12.htm Japanese Archaeological Association, 2015, "Statement by the President Calling for Preservation of the Takaozan Kofun in Numazu City, Shizuoka Prefecture"] Accessed July 8, 2017.
Additionally, the site lies in the path of the planned construction of the urban arterial road (Numazu South Isshiki Line), which Numazu City considers a critical route for the urban structure.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/takaosan/jyoukyou.htm Numazu City, "Status of Urban Arterial Road Construction for Numazu South Isshiki Line"] Accessed July 8, 2017. Consequently, debates regarding the coexistence of road construction and kofun preservation have taken place, with various measures being examined to achieve both.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/g-shigiki/g-sigiki/dayori/h27/pdf/207-10.pdf Numazu City, 2015, "Submission of a Petition Regarding the Continuation of the Takaozan Kofun" (PDF file)] Accessed July 8, 2017. [https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/takaosan/index.htm Numazu City, 2017, "Preservation of the Takaozan Kofun and Road Development"] Accessed July 8, 2017.

== Discovery of Takaozan Kofun and Its Name == [[File:Takaosan Kofun OSM 02.png|thumb|250px|Map of the surrounding area]] The tumulus area of Takaozan Kofun was once home to Kumano Shrine on the front section and Takaozan Homimi Shrine on the rear section. The Numazu City Board of Education estimates its construction to have been around the year [[250]], during the early [[Kofun period]] (the period of the [[Yamatai Kingdom]]), making it one of the oldest and largest kofun in Eastern Japan from the early appearance of such burial mounds.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/profile/bunkazai/kofun/takaosan.htm Numazu City, 2024, "Takaozan Kofun"] Accessed October 20, 2024. The [[Japanese Archaeological Association]] has evaluated it as an extremely important site for understanding the process of forming the early statehood marked by the kofun culture.[http://archaeology.jp/maibun/nikokyo2015-12.htm Japanese Archaeological Association, 2015, "Statement by the President Calling for Preservation of the Takaozan Kofun in Numazu City, Shizuoka Prefecture"] Accessed July 8, 2017.

'''Takaozan Kofun''' (Takaozan burial mound) is a [[kofun]] located in [[Higashikumando]] ("East Kumando"), [[Numazu City]], [[Shizuoka Prefecture]]. It has the form of a [[Zenpō-kōhō-fun]] (keyhole-shaped mound with a rectangular rear and trapezoidal front)Numazu City Board of Education (2012) summary report. It has been designated as a [[Historic Site]] by the national government.[https://www.bunka.go.jp/koho_hodo_oshirase/hodohappyo/94070501.html Cultural Council's Recommendation (Designation of Historic Sites, Places of Scenic Beauty, and Natural Monuments)] (Agency for Cultural Affairs press release, June 24, 2024).Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology, Notification No. 142, October 11, 2024.
The Numazu City Board of Education estimates its construction to have been around the year [[250]], during the early [[Kofun period]] (the period of the [[Yamatai Kingdom]]), making it one of the oldest and largest kofun in Eastern Japan from the early appearance of such burial mounds.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/profile/bunkazai/kofun/takaosan.htm Numazu City, 2024, "Takaozan Kofun"] Accessed October 20, 2024. The [[Japanese Archaeological Association]] has evaluated it as an extremely important site for understanding the process of forming the early statehood marked by the kofun culture.[http://archaeology.jp/maibun/nikokyo2015-12.htm Japanese Archaeological Association, 2015, "Statement by the President Calling for Preservation of the Takaozan Kofun in Numazu City, Shizuoka Prefecture"] Accessed July 8, 2017.
Additionally, the site lies in the path of the planned construction of the urban arterial road (Numazu South Isshiki Line), which Numazu City considers a critical route for the urban structure.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/takaosan/jyoukyou.htm Numazu City, "Status of Urban Arterial Road Construction for Numazu South Isshiki Line"] Accessed July 8, 2017. Consequently, debates regarding the coexistence of road construction and kofun preservation have taken place, with various measures being examined to achieve both.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/g-shigiki/g-sigiki/dayori/h27/pdf/207-10.pdf Numazu City, 2015, "Submission of a Petition Regarding the Continuation of the Takaozan Kofun" (PDF file)] Accessed July 8, 2017. [https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/takaosan/index.htm Numazu City, 2017, "Preservation of the Takaozan Kofun and Road Development"] Accessed July 8, 2017.
== Discovery of Takaozan Kofun and Its Name == [[File:Takaosan Kofun OSM 02.png|thumb|250px|Map of the surrounding area]] The tumulus area of Takaozan Kofun was once home to Kumano Shrine on the front section and Takaozan Homimi Shrine on the rear section. Notably, Takaozan Homimi Shrine stood atop a square plateau, which led to speculation that it was built on an ancient burial mound.Numazu City Board of Education (2012) p. 10, Yamamoto (2012) p. 119
Shinichi Ono, an archaeologist with [[Kato Academy (Shizuoka Prefecture)]], hypothesized that the shrine was located on a tumulus while conducting site investigations in the 1960s associated with the construction of the [[Tōmei Expressway]]."Ah, the Takaozan Kofun: A Cultural Asset Worth Preserving" Numazu Asahi Newspaper, July 2, 2015, front page. In his 1978 publication "Numazu City History in Pictures," Ono introduced the name "Takaozan Kofun," referencing the Homimi Shrine, and classified the tumulus as a [[square tomb]]. However, when Numazu City registered it as an archaeological site, it was recorded under the local name "Tsubahata Kofun."The specific timing of the registration varies between sections of the 2012 excavation report by the Numazu City Board of Education: the preface states 1982, while p. 10 indicates 1979. Due to these inconsistencies, the year is not specified here. However, "Tsubahata" refers to the area north of the tumulus, while the correct local name of Takaozan Kofun is "Hokuhō."Ono (1978) p. 31, Numazu City Board of Education (2012) preface, p. 10
Despite being registered as an archaeological site, no significant investigations were conducted, and no artifacts associated with the tumulus were identified until the construction of the Numazu South Isshiki Line advanced in the Heisei era (1989–2019). By 2005, land acquisitions in the Kumano Shrine and Takaozan Homimi Shrine area were completed. Both shrines were relocated eastward, and concerns arose about the tumulus's existence under Takaozan Homimi Shrine. Consequently, test excavations commenced in 2005, identifying ditch structures and [[haji earthenware]], suggesting the possibility of a square tomb.Numazu City Board of Education (2012) p. 10
From 2007 to 2009, a second round of excavations and a full-scale investigation were conducted, leading to the conclusion that the site was a zenpō-kōhō-fun constructed during the 3rd century, similar to the [[Kōbōzan Kofun]] in [[Matsumoto City]], [[Nagano Prefecture]]. In 2011, the name "Takaozan Kofun," first proposed by Ono, was officially adopted.Numazu City Board of Education (2012) preface, pp. 10–14, Takizawa (2013) p. 5
In 2014, further investigations were conducted to confirm the tumulus's construction date and evaluate the possibility of additional burial facilities.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/pr/interview/pdf/201408_3.pdf Numazu City, 2014, "Results of Additional Excavations at Takaozan Kofun" (PDF file)] Accessed July 6, 2017.
== Location and Environment of the Kofun == [[File:Ashitaka Volcano Relief Map, SRTM-1 and Takaozan kofun.jpg|thumb|300px|Relief map of Mount Ashitaka and surrounding areas. The red circle marks Takaozan Kofun's location, while the southeast area shaded white represents the former Ukishima Marsh.]] Takaozan Kofun is situated at the terminus of a ridge

[[Takaosan Kofun]]{{Expand Japanese}} {{Otheruses||Kofun on Mount Takao in Kashiwara City, Osaka Prefecture (Takaozan Site)|Takaozan (Osaka Prefecture)}} {{{{Infobox ancient site |name = Takaozan Kofun |image = [[File:Takaosan-kofun (Numazu) zenkei.JPG|280px]]Full view of the tumulus (foreground left: front section, background right: rear section)(as of June 2015) |location = [[Higashikumando]], [[Numazu City]], [[Shizuoka Prefecture]] |latitude = 35|latitude_min = 7|latitude_sec = 22.73 |longitude =138|longitude_min = 51|longitude_sec = 40.22 |ISO = JP-22 |shape = [[Zenpō-kōhō-fun]] |dimensions = Tumulus length: 62mHeight: 4.7m (estimated at approximately 5m) |burial_facility = [[Wooden coffin]] direct burial |construction_date = Around the year [[250]] |buried_person = |grave_goods = Bronze mirror (animal belt mirror of the embossed style from the Shangfang Workshop) 1 piece, magatama 1 piece, spear 1 piece, 32 iron arrowheads, 1 spearhead-plane, and a large amount of earthenware from the tumulus and the surrounding ditch. |cultural_property_designation = [[Historic Site]] designated by the national government ("Takaozan Kofun") |notable_features = |map = Japan Shizuoka |icon = Zenpō-kōhō-fun - South }} {{osm box|n|4735442868}}
'''Takaozan Kofun''' (Takaozan burial mound) is a [[kofun]] located in [[Higashikumando]] ("East Kumando"), [[Numazu City]], [[Shizuoka Prefecture]]. It has the form of a [[Zenpō-kōhō-fun]] (keyhole-shaped mound with a rectangular rear and trapezoidal front)Numazu City Board of Education (2012) summary report. It has been designated as a [[Historic Site]] by the national government.[https://www.bunka.go.jp/koho_hodo_oshirase/hodohappyo/94070501.html Cultural Council's Recommendation (Designation of Historic Sites, Places of Scenic Beauty, and Natural Monuments)] (Agency for Cultural Affairs press release, June 24, 2024).Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology, Notification No. 142, October 11, 2024.
The Numazu City Board of Education estimates its construction to have been around the year [[250]], during the early [[Kofun period]] (the period of the [[Yamatai Kingdom]]), making it one of the oldest and largest kofun in Eastern Japan from the early appearance of such burial mounds.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/profile/bunkazai/kofun/takaosan.htm Numazu City, 2024, "Takaozan Kofun"] Accessed October 20, 2024. The [[Japanese Archaeological Association]] has evaluated it as an extremely important site for understanding the process of forming the early statehood marked by the kofun culture.[http://archaeology.jp/maibun/nikokyo2015-12.htm Japanese Archaeological Association, 2015, "Statement by the President Calling for Preservation of the Takaozan Kofun in Numazu City, Shizuoka Prefecture"] Accessed July 8, 2017.
Additionally, the site lies in the path of the planned construction of the urban arterial road (Numazu South Isshiki Line), which Numazu City considers a critical route for the urban structure.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/takaosan/jyoukyou.htm Numazu City, "Status of Urban Arterial Road Construction for Numazu South Isshiki Line"] Accessed July 8, 2017. Consequently, debates regarding the coexistence of road construction and kofun preservation have taken place, with various measures being examined to achieve both.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/g-shigiki/g-sigiki/dayori/h27/pdf/207-10.pdf Numazu City, 2015, "Submission of a Petition Regarding the Continuation of the Takaozan Kofun" (PDF file)] Accessed July 8, 2017. [https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/takaosan/index.htm Numazu City, 2017, "Preservation of the Takaozan Kofun and Road Development"] Accessed July 8, 2017.
== Discovery of Takaozan Kofun and Its name == [[File:Takaosan Kofun OSM 02.png|thumb|250px|Map of the surrounding area]] The tumulus area of Takaozan Kofun was once home to Kumano Shrine on the front section and Takaozan Homimi Shrine on the rear section. Notably, Takaozan Homimi Shrine stood atop a square plateau, which led to speculation that it was built on an ancient burial mound.Numazu City Board of Education (2012) p. 10, Yamamoto (2012) p. 119
Shinichi Ono, an archaeologist with [[Kato Academy (Shizuoka Prefecture)]], hypothesized that the shrine was located on a tumulus while conducting site investigations in the 1960s associated with the construction of the [[Tōmei Expressway]]."Ah, the Takaozan Kofun: A Cultural Asset Worth Preserving" Numazu Asahi Newspaper, July 2, 2015, front page. In his 1978 publication "Numazu City History in Pictures," Ono introduced the name "Takaozan Kofun," referencing the Homimi Shrine, and classified the tumulus as a [[square tomb]]. However, when Numazu City registered it as an archaeological site, it was recorded under the local name "Tsubahata Kofun."The specific timing of the registration varies between sections of the 2012 excavation report by the Numazu City Board of Education: the preface states 1982, while p. 10 indicates 1979. Due to these inconsistencies, the year is not specified here. However, "Tsubahata" refers to the area north of the tumulus, while the correct local name of Takaozan Kofun is "Hokuhō."Ono (1978) p. 31, Numazu City Board of Education (2012) preface, p. 10
Despite being registered as an archaeological site, no significant investigations were conducted, and no artifacts associated with the tumulus were identified until the construction of the Numazu South Isshiki Line advanced in the Heisei era (1989–2019). By 2005, land acquisitions in the Kumano Shrine and Takaozan Homimi Shrine area were completed. Both shrines were relocated eastward, and concerns arose about the tumulus's existence under Takaozan Homimi Shrine. Consequently, test excavations commenced in 2005, identifying ditch structures and [[haji earthenware]], suggesting the possibility of a square tomb.Numazu City Board of Education (2012) p. 10
From 2007 to 2009, a second round of excavations and a full-scale investigation were conducted, leading to the conclusion that the site was a zenpō-kōhō-fun constructed during the 3rd century, similar to the [[Kōbōzan Kofun]] in [[Matsumoto City]], [[Nagano Prefecture]]. In 2011, the name "Takaozan Kofun," first proposed by Ono, was officially adopted.Numazu City Board of Education (2012) preface, pp. 10–14, Takizawa (2013) p. 5
In 2014, further investigations were conducted to confirm the tumulus's construction date and evaluate the possibility of additional burial facilities.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/pr/interview/pdf/201408_3.pdf Numazu City, 2014, "Results of Additional Excavations at Takaozan Kofun" (PDF file)] Accessed July 6, 2017.
== location and Environment of the Kofun == [[File:Ashitaka Volcano Relief Map, SRTM-1 and Takaozan kofun.jpg|thumb|300px|Relief map of Mount Ashitaka and surrounding areas. The red circle marks Takaozan Kofun's location, while the southeast area shaded white represents the former Ukishima Marsh.]] Takaozan Kofun is situated at the terminus of a ridge

[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/takaosan/index.htm Numazu City, 2017, "Preservation of the Takaozan Kofun and Road Development"] Accessed July 8, 2017.
== Location and Environment of the Burial Mound == [[File:Ashitaka Volcano Relief Map, SRTM-1 and Takkaosan kofun.jpg|thumb|300px|Map of {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}} and its surroundings. The red circle indicates the location of Takkaosan Kofun. The lowland area to the southeast, marked in white, corresponds to the former {{ill|Ukishima Marsh|ja|浮島沼}}.]] The {{ill|Takkaosan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}} is located at the southernmost ridge extending from {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}}. The elevation at the site of the kofun is approximately 20 meters. While situated on a ridge, it cannot be regarded as a burial mound constructed on elevated terrain.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2012), p.1; Sato (2013a), p.11</ref>
{{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}} is believed to have begun activity around 400,000 years ago. From about 170,000 years ago, it actively emitted {{ill|andesite|ja|安山岩}} and {{ill|dacite|ja|デイサイト}} lava flows towards its southeastern flank, forming the gentle hills now seen in the areas of modern-day {{ill|Numazu|ja|沼津市}} City and {{ill|Nagaizumi|ja|長泉町}} Town. {{ill|Takkaosan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}} was constructed at the edge of these hills, shaped by volcanic activity that began roughly 170,000 years ago.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), pp.36; Numazu City Board of Education (2012), pp.1-4</ref>
The volcanic activity of {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}} ended about 100,000 years ago. Subsequently, the nearby {{ill|Ancient Mount Fuji|ja|古富士火山}} became active, depositing large amounts of volcanic ash on the lower slopes of Ashitaka. This ash formed thick {{ill|loam|ja|ローム層}} layers. During the latter period of Ancient Mount Fuji’s activity, an upper loam layer developed, characterized by alternating {{ill|scoria|ja|スコリア}} layers and black bands of humus soil. During this time, volcanic deposits from the {{ill|Aira Caldera|ja|姶良カルデラ}}'s massive eruption, about 25,000 years ago, also accumulated in the Ashitaka foothills, mixing with deposits from Ancient Mount Fuji to create a stratum known as pseudo-loam.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), pp.37, 67; Numazu City Board of Education (2012), p.4</ref>
After Ancient Mount Fuji became dormant, the activity of the {{ill|New Fuji Volcano|ja|新期富士火山}} began around 11,000 years ago. Initially, the volcanic activity was dominated by large lava flows, which were obstructed by {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}} and did not reach the area around {{ill|Takkaosan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}}. As a result, black soil layers developed in the Ashitaka foothills, forming the uppermost part of the loam layers. By the late {{ill|Jōmon period|ja|縄文時代}}, approximately 3,200 years ago, significant pumice eruptions occurred at {{ill|Kawago-daira|ja|カワゴ平}}, part of the {{ill|Izu East Volcano Group|ja|伊豆東部火山群}}. However, these eruptions did not leave significant layers in the Ashitaka region. During the same period, large-scale {{ill|mountain collapses|ja|山体崩壊}} occurred on the eastern slopes of Mount Fuji, creating massive debris flows that accumulated in the {{ill|Kise River|ja|黄瀬川}} basin. These events formed the {{ill|Kise River alluvial fan|ja|黄瀬川扇状地}}, transforming the eastern parts of modern-day {{ill|Numazu|ja|沼津市}} City from wetlands into dry land by the start of the {{ill|Yayoi period|ja|弥生時代}}.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), p.38; Numazu City Board of Education (2012), pp.1-4</ref>
On the other hand, during the {{ill|Jōmon transgression|ja|縄文海進}}, the sea reached the foothills of {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}}. Subsequently, as the sea receded, sandbars formed along the {{ill|Kano River|ja|狩野川}}’s estuary, creating a water body between the Ashitaka foothills and the sandbars. This became the prototype for {{ill|Ukishima Marsh|ja|浮島沼}}. Over time, this water body transitioned from a brackish lagoon to a marshland and then to a wetland. During the construction of {{ill|Takkaosan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}}, boats could navigate to within 2–3 kilometers southwest of the kofun.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), p.1; Numazu City Cultural Heritage Center (2016), p.3</ref>
Finally, from the very end of the {{ill|Yayoi period|ja|弥生時代}} to the early {{ill|Kofun period|ja|古墳時代}}, new scoria layers were deposited on the Ashitaka foothills, including the area around {{ill|Takkaosan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}}. The rear mound of {{ill|Takkaosan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}} was constructed directly atop these new scoria layers.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), pp.4, 15</ref>

The red circle marks Takaozan Kofun's location, while the southeast area shaded white represents the former Ukishima Marsh.]] Takaozan Kofun is situated at the terminus of a ridge

On the other hand, during the {{ill|Jōmon transgression|ja|縄文海進}}, the sea reached the foothills of {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}}. Subsequently, as the sea receded, sandbars formed along the {{ill|Kano River|ja|狩野川}}’s estuary, creating a water body between the Ashitaka foothills and the sandbars. This became the prototype for {{ill|Ukishima Marsh|ja|浮島沼}}. Over time, this water body transitioned from a brackish lagoon to a marshland and then to a wetland. During the construction of {{ill|Takkaosan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}}, boats could navigate to within 2–3 kilometers southwest of the kofun.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), p.1; Numazu City Cultural Heritage Center (2016), p.3</ref>
Finally, from the very end of the {{ill|Yayoi period|ja|弥生時代}} to the early {{ill|Kofun period|ja|古墳時代}}, new scoria layers were deposited on the Ashitaka foothills, including the area around {{ill|Takkaosan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}}. The rear mound of {{ill|Takkaosan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}} was constructed directly atop these new scoria layers.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), pp.4, 15</ref>

[[Takaosan Kofun]]{{Expand Japanese}} {{Otheruses||Kofun on Mount Takao in Kashiwara City, Osaka Prefecture (Takaozan Site)|Takaozan (Osaka Prefecture)}} {{{{Infobox ancient site |name = Takaozan Kofun |image = [[File:Takaosan-kofun (Numazu) zenkei.JPG|280px]]Full view of the tumulus (foreground left: front section, background right: rear section)(as of June 2015) |location = [[Higashikumando]], [[Numazu City]], [[Shizuoka Prefecture]] |latitude = 35|latitude_min = 7|latitude_sec = 22.73 |longitude =138|longitude_min = 51|longitude_sec = 40.22 |ISO = JP-22 |shape = [[Zenpō-kōhō-fun]] |dimensions = Tumulus length: 62mHeight: 4.7m (estimated at approximately 5m) |burial_facility = [[Wooden coffin]] direct burial |construction_date = Around the year [[250]] |buried_person = |grave_goods = Bronze mirror (animal belt mirror of the embossed style from the Shangfang Workshop) 1 piece, magatama 1 piece, spear 1 piece, 32 iron arrowheads, 1 spearhead-plane, and a large amount of earthenware from the tumulus and the surrounding ditch. |cultural_property_designation = [[Historic Site]] designated by the national government ("Takaozan Kofun") |notable_features = |map = Japan Shizuoka |icon = Zenpō-kōhō-fun - South }} {{osm box|n|4735442868}}
'''Takaozan Kofun''' (Takaozan burial mound) is a [[kofun]] located in [[Higashikumando]] ("East Kumando"), [[Numazu City]], [[Shizuoka Prefecture]]. It has the form of a [[Zenpō-kōhō-fun]] (keyhole-shaped mound with a rectangular rear and trapezoidal front)Numazu City Board of Education (2012) summary report. It has been designated as a [[Historic Site]] by the national government.[https://www.bunka.go.jp/koho_hodo_oshirase/hodohappyo/94070501.html Cultural Council's Recommendation (Designation of Historic Sites, Places of Scenic Beauty, and Natural Monuments)] (Agency for Cultural Affairs press release, June 24, 2024).Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology, Notification No. 142, October 11, 2024.
The Numazu City Board of Education estimates its construction to have been around the year [[250]], during the early [[Kofun period]] (the period of the [[Yamatai Kingdom]]), making it one of the oldest and largest kofun in Eastern Japan from the early appearance of such burial mounds.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/profile/bunkazai/kofun/takaosan.htm Numazu City, 2024, "Takaozan Kofun"] Accessed October 20, 2024. The [[Japanese Archaeological Association]] has evaluated it as an extremely important site for understanding the process of forming the early statehood marked by the kofun culture.[http://archaeology.jp/maibun/nikokyo2015-12.htm Japanese Archaeological Association, 2015, "Statement by the President Calling for Preservation of the Takaozan Kofun in Numazu City, Shizuoka Prefecture"] Accessed July 8, 2017.
Additionally, the site lies in the path of the planned construction of the urban arterial road (Numazu South Isshiki Line), which Numazu City considers a critical route for the urban structure.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/takaosan/jyoukyou.htm Numazu City, "Status of Urban Arterial Road Construction for Numazu South Isshiki Line"] Accessed July 8, 2017. Consequently, debates regarding the coexistence of road construction and kofun preservation have taken place, with various measures being examined to achieve both.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/g-shigiki/g-sigiki/dayori/h27/pdf/207-10.pdf Numazu City, 2015, "Submission of a Petition Regarding the Continuation of the Takaozan Kofun" (PDF file)] Accessed July 8, 2017. [https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/takaosan/index.htm Numazu City, 2017, "Preservation of the Takaozan Kofun and Road Development"] Accessed July 8, 2017.
== Location and Environment of the Burial Mound == [[File:Ashitaka Volcano Relief Map, SRTM-1 and Takkaosan kofun.jpg|thumb|300px|Map of {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}} and its surroundings. The red circle indicates the location of Takkaosan Kofun. The lowland area to the southeast, marked in white, corresponds to the former {{ill|Ukishima Marsh|ja|浮島沼}}.]] The {{ill|Takkaosan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}} is located at the southernmost ridge extending from {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}}. The elevation at the site of the kofun is approximately 20 meters. While situated on a ridge, it cannot be regarded as a burial mound constructed on elevated terrain.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2012), p.1; Sato (2013a), p.11</ref>
{{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}} is believed to have begun activity around 400,000 years ago. From about 170,000 years ago, it actively emitted {{ill|andesite|ja|安山岩}} and {{ill|dacite|ja|デイサイト}} lava flows towards its southeastern flank, forming the gentle hills now seen in the areas of modern-day {{ill|Numazu|ja|沼津市}} City and {{ill|Nagaizumi|ja|長泉町}} Town. {{ill|Takkaosan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}} was constructed at the edge of these hills, shaped by volcanic activity that began roughly 170,000 years ago.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), pp.36; Numazu City Board of Education (2012), pp.1-4</ref>
The volcanic activity of {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}} ended about 100,000 years ago. Subsequently, the nearby {{ill|Ancient Mount Fuji|ja|古富士火山}} became active, depositing large amounts of volcanic ash on the lower slopes of Ashitaka. This ash formed thick {{ill|loam|ja|ローム層}} layers. During the latter period of Ancient Mount Fuji’s activity, an upper loam layer developed, characterized by alternating {{ill|scoria|ja|スコリア}} layers and black bands of humus soil. During this time, volcanic deposits from the {{ill|Aira Caldera|ja|姶良カルデラ}}'s massive eruption, about 25,000 years ago, also accumulated in the Ashitaka foothills, mixing with deposits from Ancient Mount Fuji to create a stratum known as pseudo-loam.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), pp.37, 67; Numazu City Board of Education (2012), p.4</ref>
After Ancient Mount Fuji became dormant, the activity of the {{ill|New Fuji Volcano|ja|新期富士火山}} began around 11,000 years ago. Initially, the volcanic activity was dominated by large lava flows, which were obstructed by {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}} and did not reach the area around {{ill|Takkaosan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}}. As a result, black soil layers developed in the Ashitaka foothills, forming the uppermost part of the loam layers. By the late {{ill|Jōmon period|ja|縄文時代}}, approximately 3,200 years ago, significant pumice eruptions occurred at {{ill|Kawago-daira|ja|カワゴ平}}, part of the {{ill|Izu East Volcano Group|ja|伊豆東部火山群}}. However, these eruptions did not leave significant layers in the Ashitaka region. During the same period, large-scale {{ill|mountain collapses|ja|山体崩壊}} occurred on the eastern slopes of Mount Fuji, creating massive debris flows that accumulated in the {{ill|Kise River|ja|黄瀬川}} basin. These events formed the {{ill|Kise River alluvial fan|ja|黄瀬川扇状地}}, transforming the eastern parts of modern-day {{ill|Numazu|ja|沼津市}} City from wetlands into dry land by the start of the {{ill|Yayoi period|ja|弥生時代}}.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), p.38; Numazu City Board of Education (2012), pp.1-4</ref>
On the other hand, during the {{ill|Jōmon transgression|ja|縄文海進}}, the sea reached the foothills of {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}}. Subsequently, as the sea receded, sandbars formed along the {{ill|Kano River|ja|狩野川}}’s estuary, creating a water body between the Ashitaka foothills and the sandbars. This became the prototype for {{ill|Ukishima Marsh|ja|浮島沼}}. Over time, this water body transitioned from a brackish lagoon to a marshland and then to a wetland. During the construction of {{ill|Takkaosan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}}, boats could navigate to within 2–3 kilometers southwest of the kofun.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), p.1; Numazu City Cultural Heritage Center (2016), p.3</ref>
Finally, from the very end of the {{ill|Yayoi period|ja|弥生時代}} to the early {{ill|Kofun period|ja|古墳時代}}, new scoria layers were deposited on the Ashitaka foothills, including the area around {{ill|Takkaosan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}}. The rear mound of {{ill|Takkaosan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}} was constructed directly atop these new scoria layers.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), pp.4, 15</ref>

Additionally, the site lies in the path of the planned construction of the urban arterial road (Numazu South Isshiki Line), which Numazu City considers a critical route for the urban structure.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/takaosan/jyoukyou.htm Numazu City, "Status of Urban Arterial Road Construction for Numazu South Isshiki Line"] Accessed July 8, 2017. Consequently, debates regarding the coexistence of road construction and kofun preservation have taken place, with various measures being examined to achieve both.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/g-shigiki/g-sigiki/dayori/h27/pdf/207-10.pdf Numazu City, 2015, "Submission of a Petition Regarding the Continuation of the Takaozan Kofun" (PDF file)] Accessed July 8, 2017. [https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/takaosan/index.htm Numazu City, 2017, "Preservation of the Takaozan Kofun and Road Development"] Accessed July 8, 2017.
== Location and Environment of the Burial Mound == [[File:Ashitaka Volcano Relief Map, SRTM-1 and Takkaosan kofun.jpg|thumb|300px|Map of {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}} and its surroundings. The red circle indicates the location of Takaozan Kofun. The lowland area to the southeast, marked in white, corresponds to the former {{ill|Ukishima Marsh|ja|浮島沼}}.]] The {{ill|Takaozan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}} is located at the southernmost ridge extending from {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}}. The elevation at the site of the kofun is approximately 20 meters. While situated on a ridge, it cannot be regarded as a burial mound constructed on elevated terrain.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2012), p.1; Sato (2013a), p.11</ref>
{{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}} is believed to have begun activity around 400,000 years ago. From about 170,000 years ago, it actively emitted {{ill|andesite|ja|安山岩}} and {{ill|dacite|ja|デイサイト}} lava flows towards its southeastern flank, forming the gentle hills now seen in the areas of modern-day {{ill|Numazu|ja|沼津市}} City and {{ill|Nagaizumi|ja|長泉町}} Town. {{ill|Takaozan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}} was constructed at the edge of these hills, shaped by volcanic activity that began roughly 170,000 years ago.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), pp.36; Numazu City Board of Education (2012), pp.1-4</ref>
The volcanic activity of {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}} ended about 100,000 years ago. Subsequently, the nearby {{ill|Ancient Mount Fuji|ja|古富士火山}} became active, depositing large amounts of volcanic ash on the lower slopes of Ashitaka. This ash formed thick {{ill|loam|ja|ローム層}} layers. During the latter period of Ancient Mount Fuji’s activity, an upper loam layer developed, characterized by alternating {{ill|scoria|ja|スコリア}} layers and black bands of humus soil. During this time, volcanic deposits from the {{ill|Aira Caldera|ja|姶良カルデラ}}'s massive eruption, about 25,000 years ago, also accumulated in the Ashitaka foothills, mixing with deposits from Ancient Mount Fuji to create a stratum known as pseudo-loam.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), pp.37, 67; Numazu City Board of Education (2012), p.4</ref>
After Ancient Mount Fuji became dormant, the activity of the {{ill|New Fuji Volcano|ja|新期富士火山}} began around 11,000 years ago. Initially, the volcanic activity was dominated by large lava flows, which were obstructed by {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}} and did not reach the area around {{ill|Takaozan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}}. As a result, black soil layers developed in the Ashitaka foothills, forming the uppermost part of the loam layers. By the late {{ill|Jōmon period|ja|縄文時代}}, approximately 3,200 years ago, significant pumice eruptions occurred at {{ill|Kawago-daira|ja|カワゴ平}}, part of the {{ill|Izu East Volcano Group|ja|伊豆東部火山群}}. However, these eruptions did not leave significant layers in the Ashitaka region. During the same period, large-scale {{ill|mountain collapses|ja|山体崩壊}} occurred on the eastern slopes of Mount Fuji, creating massive debris flows that accumulated in the {{ill|Kise River|ja|黄瀬川}} basin. These events formed the {{ill|Kise River alluvial fan|ja|黄瀬川扇状地}}, transforming the eastern parts of modern-day {{ill|Numazu|ja|沼津市}} City from wetlands into dry land by the start of the {{ill|Yayoi period|ja|弥生時代}}.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), p.38; Numazu City Board of Education (2012), pp.1-4</ref>
On the other hand, during the {{ill|Jōmon transgression|ja|縄文海進}}, the sea reached the foothills of {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}}. Subsequently, as the sea receded, sandbars formed along the {{ill|Kano River|ja|狩野川}}’s estuary, creating a water body between the Ashitaka foothills and the sandbars. This became the prototype for {{ill|Ukishima Marsh|ja|浮島沼}}. Over time, this water body transitioned from a brackish lagoon to a marshland and then to a wetland. During the construction of {{ill|Takaozan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}}, boats could navigate to within 2–3 kilometers southwest of the kofun.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), p.1; Numazu City Cultural Heritage Center (2016), p.3</ref>
Finally, from the very end of the {{ill|Yayoi period|ja|弥生時代}} to the early {{ill|Kofun period|ja|古墳時代}}, new scoria layers were deposited on the Ashitaka foothills, including the area around {{ill|Takaozan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}}. The rear mound of {{ill|Takaozan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}} was constructed directly atop these new scoria layers.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), pp.4, 15</ref>
== location and Environment of the Kofun == [[File:Ashitaka Volcano Relief Map, SRTM-1 and Takaozan kofun.jpg|thumb|300px|Relief map of Mount Ashitaka and surrounding areas. The red circle marks Takaozan Kofun's location, while the southeast area shaded white represents the former Ukishima Marsh.]] Takaozan Kofun is situated at the terminus of a ridge

It has the form of a [[Zenpō-kōhō-fun]] (keyhole-shaped mound with a rectangular rear and trapezoidal front)Numazu City Board of Education (2012) summary report. It has been designated as a [[Historic Site]] by the national government.[https://www.bunka.go.jp/koho_hodo_oshirase/hodohappyo/94070501.html Cultural Council's Recommendation (Designation of Historic Sites, Places of Scenic Beauty, and Natural Monuments)] (Agency for Cultural Affairs press release, June 24, 2024).Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology, Notification No. 142, October 11, 2024.
The Numazu City Board of Education estimates its construction to have been around the year [[250]], during the early [[Kofun period]] (the period of the [[Yamatai Kingdom]]), making it one of the oldest and largest kofun in Eastern Japan from the early appearance of such burial mounds.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/profile/bunkazai/kofun/takaosan.htm Numazu City, 2024, "Takaozan Kofun"] Accessed October 20, 2024. The [[Japanese Archaeological Association]] has evaluated it as an extremely important site for understanding the process of forming the early statehood marked by the kofun culture.[http://archaeology.jp/maibun/nikokyo2015-12.htm Japanese Archaeological Association, 2015, "Statement by the President Calling for Preservation of the Takaozan Kofun in Numazu City, Shizuoka Prefecture"] Accessed July 8, 2017.
Additionally, the site lies in the path of the planned construction of the urban arterial road (Numazu South Isshiki Line), which Numazu City considers a critical route for the urban structure.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/takaosan/jyoukyou.htm Numazu City, "Status of Urban Arterial Road Construction for Numazu South Isshiki Line"] Accessed July 8, 2017. Consequently, debates regarding the coexistence of road construction and kofun preservation have taken place, with various measures being examined to achieve both.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/g-shigiki/g-sigiki/dayori/h27/pdf/207-10.pdf Numazu City, 2015, "Submission of a Petition Regarding the Continuation of the Takaozan Kofun" (PDF file)] Accessed July 8, 2017. [https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/takaosan/index.htm Numazu City, 2017, "Preservation of the Takaozan Kofun and Road Development"] Accessed July 8, 2017.

[[Takaosan Kofun]]{{Expand Japanese}} {{Otheruses||Kofun on Mount Takao in Kashiwara City, Osaka Prefecture (Takaozan Site)|Takaozan (Osaka Prefecture)}} {{{{Infobox ancient site |name = Takaozan Kofun |image = [[File:Takaosan-kofun (Numazu) zenkei.JPG|280px]]Full view of the tumulus (foreground left: front section, background right: rear section)(as of June 2015) |location = [[Higashikumando]], [[Numazu City]], [[Shizuoka Prefecture]] |latitude = 35|latitude_min = 7|latitude_sec = 22.73 |longitude =138|longitude_min = 51|longitude_sec = 40.22 |ISO = JP-22 |shape = [[Zenpō-kōhō-fun]] |dimensions = Tumulus length: 62mHeight: 4.7m (estimated at approximately 5m) |burial_facility = [[Wooden coffin]] direct burial |construction_date = Around the year [[250]] |buried_person = |grave_goods = Bronze mirror (animal belt mirror of the embossed style from the Shangfang Workshop) 1 piece, magatama 1 piece, spear 1 piece, 32 iron arrowheads, 1 spearhead-plane, and a large amount of earthenware from the tumulus and the surrounding ditch. |cultural_property_designation = [[Historic Site]] designated by the national government ("Takaozan Kofun") |notable_features = |map = Japan Shizuoka |icon = Zenpō-kōhō-fun - South }} {{osm box|n|4735442868}}
'''Takaozan Kofun''' (Takaozan burial mound) is a [[kofun]] located in [[Higashikumando]] ("East Kumando"), [[Numazu City]], [[Shizuoka Prefecture]]. It has the form of a [[Zenpō-kōhō-fun]] (keyhole-shaped mound with a rectangular rear and trapezoidal front)Numazu City Board of Education (2012) summary report. It has been designated as a [[Historic Site]] by the national government.[https://www.bunka.go.jp/koho_hodo_oshirase/hodohappyo/94070501.html Cultural Council's Recommendation (Designation of Historic Sites, Places of Scenic Beauty, and Natural Monuments)] (Agency for Cultural Affairs press release, June 24, 2024).Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology, Notification No. 142, October 11, 2024.
The Numazu City Board of Education estimates its construction to have been around the year [[250]], during the early [[Kofun period]] (the period of the [[Yamatai Kingdom]]), making it one of the oldest and largest kofun in Eastern Japan from the early appearance of such burial mounds.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/profile/bunkazai/kofun/takaosan.htm Numazu City, 2024, "Takaozan Kofun"] Accessed October 20, 2024. The [[Japanese Archaeological Association]] has evaluated it as an extremely important site for understanding the process of forming the early statehood marked by the kofun culture.[http://archaeology.jp/maibun/nikokyo2015-12.htm Japanese Archaeological Association, 2015, "Statement by the President Calling for Preservation of the Takaozan Kofun in Numazu City, Shizuoka Prefecture"] Accessed July 8, 2017.
Additionally, the site lies in the path of the planned construction of the urban arterial road (Numazu South Isshiki Line), which Numazu City considers a critical route for the urban structure.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/takaosan/jyoukyou.htm Numazu City, "Status of Urban Arterial Road Construction for Numazu South Isshiki Line"] Accessed July 8, 2017. Consequently, debates regarding the coexistence of road construction and kofun preservation have taken place, with various measures being examined to achieve both.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/g-shigiki/g-sigiki/dayori/h27/pdf/207-10.pdf Numazu City, 2015, "Submission of a Petition Regarding the Continuation of the Takaozan Kofun" (PDF file)] Accessed July 8, 2017. [https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/takaosan/index.htm Numazu City, 2017, "Preservation of the Takaozan Kofun and Road Development"] Accessed July 8, 2017.
== Location and Environment of the Burial Mound == [[File:Ashitaka Volcano Relief Map, SRTM-1 and Takkaosan kofun.jpg|thumb|300px|Map of {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}} and its surroundings. The red circle indicates the location of Takaozan Kofun. The lowland area to the southeast, marked in white, corresponds to the former {{ill|Ukishima Marsh|ja|浮島沼}}.]] The {{ill|Takaozan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}} is located at the southernmost ridge extending from {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}}. The elevation at the site of the kofun is approximately 20 meters. While situated on a ridge, it cannot be regarded as a burial mound constructed on elevated terrain.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2012), p.1; Sato (2013a), p.11</ref>
{{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}} is believed to have begun activity around 400,000 years ago. From about 170,000 years ago, it actively emitted {{ill|andesite|ja|安山岩}} and {{ill|dacite|ja|デイサイト}} lava flows towards its southeastern flank, forming the gentle hills now seen in the areas of modern-day {{ill|Numazu|ja|沼津市}} City and {{ill|Nagaizumi|ja|長泉町}} Town. {{ill|Takaozan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}} was constructed at the edge of these hills, shaped by volcanic activity that began roughly 170,000 years ago.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), pp.36; Numazu City Board of Education (2012), pp.1-4</ref>
The volcanic activity of {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}} ended about 100,000 years ago. Subsequently, the nearby {{ill|Ancient Mount Fuji|ja|古富士火山}} became active, depositing large amounts of volcanic ash on the lower slopes of Ashitaka. This ash formed thick {{ill|loam|ja|ローム層}} layers. During the latter period of Ancient Mount Fuji’s activity, an upper loam layer developed, characterized by alternating {{ill|scoria|ja|スコリア}} layers and black bands of humus soil. During this time, volcanic deposits from the {{ill|Aira Caldera|ja|姶良カルデラ}}'s massive eruption, about 25,000 years ago, also accumulated in the Ashitaka foothills, mixing with deposits from Ancient Mount Fuji to create a stratum known as pseudo-loam.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), pp.37, 67; Numazu City Board of Education (2012), p.4</ref>
After Ancient Mount Fuji became dormant, the activity of the {{ill|New Fuji Volcano|ja|新期富士火山}} began around 11,000 years ago. Initially, the volcanic activity was dominated by large lava flows, which were obstructed by {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}} and did not reach the area around {{ill|Takaozan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}}. As a result, black soil layers developed in the Ashitaka foothills, forming the uppermost part of the loam layers. By the late {{ill|Jōmon period|ja|縄文時代}}, approximately 3,200 years ago, significant pumice eruptions occurred at {{ill|Kawago-daira|ja|カワゴ平}}, part of the {{ill|Izu East Volcano Group|ja|伊豆東部火山群}}. However, these eruptions did not leave significant layers in the Ashitaka region. During the same period, large-scale {{ill|mountain collapses|ja|山体崩壊}} occurred on the eastern slopes of Mount Fuji, creating massive debris flows that accumulated in the {{ill|Kise River|ja|黄瀬川}} basin. These events formed the {{ill|Kise River alluvial fan|ja|黄瀬川扇状地}}, transforming the eastern parts of modern-day {{ill|Numazu|ja|沼津市}} City from wetlands into dry land by the start of the {{ill|Yayoi period|ja|弥生時代}}.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), p.38; Numazu City Board of Education (2012), pp.1-4</ref>
On the other hand, during the {{ill|Jōmon transgression|ja|縄文海進}}, the sea reached the foothills of {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}}. Subsequently, as the sea receded, sandbars formed along the {{ill|Kano River|ja|狩野川}}’s estuary, creating a water body between the Ashitaka foothills and the sandbars. This became the prototype for {{ill|Ukishima Marsh|ja|浮島沼}}. Over time, this water body transitioned from a brackish lagoon to a marshland and then to a wetland. During the construction of {{ill|Takaozan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}}, boats could navigate to within 2–3 kilometers southwest of the kofun.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), p.1; Numazu City Cultural Heritage Center (2016), p.3</ref>
Finally, from the very end of the {{ill|Yayoi period|ja|弥生時代}} to the early {{ill|Kofun period|ja|古墳時代}}, new scoria layers were deposited on the Ashitaka foothills, including the area around {{ill|Takaozan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}}. The rear mound of {{ill|Takaozan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}} was constructed directly atop these new scoria layers.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), pp.4, 15</ref>

The red circle marks Takaozan Kofun's location, while the southeast area shaded white represents the former Ukishima Marsh.]] Takaozan Kofun is situated at the terminus of a ridge

Consequently, debates regarding the coexistence of road construction and kofun preservation have taken place, with various measures being examined to achieve both.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/g-shigiki/g-sigiki/dayori/h27/pdf/207-10.pdf Numazu City, 2015, "Submission of a Petition Regarding the Continuation of the Takaozan Kofun" (PDF file)] Accessed July 8, 2017. [https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/takaosan/index.htm Numazu City, 2017, "Preservation of the Takaozan Kofun and Road Development"] Accessed July 8, 2017.
== Location and Environment of the Burial Mound == [[File:Ashitaka Volcano Relief Map, SRTM-1 and Takkaosan kofun.jpg|thumb|300px|Map of {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}} and its surroundings. The red circle indicates the location of Takaozan Kofun. The lowland area to the southeast, marked in white, corresponds to the former {{ill|Ukishima Marsh|ja|浮島沼}}.]] The {{ill|Takaozan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}} is located at the southernmost ridge extending from {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}}. The elevation at the site of the kofun is approximately 20 meters. While situated on a ridge, it cannot be regarded as a burial mound constructed on elevated terrain.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2012), p.1; Sato (2013a), p.11</ref>
{{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}} is believed to have begun activity around 400,000 years ago. From about 170,000 years ago, it actively emitted {{ill|andesite|ja|安山岩}} and {{ill|dacite|ja|デイサイト}} lava flows towards its southeastern flank, forming the gentle hills now seen in the areas of modern-day {{ill|Numazu|ja|沼津市}} City and {{ill|Nagaizumi|ja|長泉町}} Town. {{ill|Takaozan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}} was constructed at the edge of these hills, shaped by volcanic activity that began roughly 170,000 years ago.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), pp.36; Numazu City Board of Education (2012), pp.1-4</ref>
The volcanic activity of {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}} ended about 100,000 years ago. Subsequently, the nearby {{ill|Ancient Mount Fuji|ja|古富士火山}} became active, depositing large amounts of volcanic ash on the lower slopes of Ashitaka. This ash formed thick {{ill|loam|ja|ローム層}} layers. During the latter period of Ancient Mount Fuji’s activity, an upper loam layer developed, characterized by alternating {{ill|scoria|ja|スコリア}} layers and black bands of humus soil. During this time, volcanic deposits from the {{ill|Aira Caldera|ja|姶良カルデラ}}'s massive eruption, about 25,000 years ago, also accumulated in the Ashitaka foothills, mixing with deposits from Ancient Mount Fuji to create a stratum known as pseudo-loam.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), pp.37, 67; Numazu City Board of Education (2012), p.4</ref>
After Ancient Mount Fuji became dormant, the activity of the {{ill|New Fuji Volcano|ja|新期富士火山}} began around 11,000 years ago. Initially, the volcanic activity was dominated by large lava flows, which were obstructed by {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}} and did not reach the area around {{ill|Takaozan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}}. As a result, black soil layers developed in the Ashitaka foothills, forming the uppermost part of the loam layers. By the late {{ill|Jōmon period|ja|縄文時代}}, approximately 3,200 years ago, significant pumice eruptions occurred at {{ill|Kawago-daira|ja|カワゴ平}}, part of the {{ill|Izu East Volcano Group|ja|伊豆東部火山群}}. However, these eruptions did not leave significant layers in the Ashitaka region. During the same period, large-scale {{ill|mountain collapses|ja|山体崩壊}} occurred on the eastern slopes of Mount Fuji, creating massive debris flows that accumulated in the {{ill|Kise River|ja|黄瀬川}} basin. These events formed the {{ill|Kise River alluvial fan|ja|黄瀬川扇状地}}, transforming the eastern parts of modern-day {{ill|Numazu|ja|沼津市}} City from wetlands into dry land by the start of the {{ill|Yayoi period|ja|弥生時代}}.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), p.38; Numazu City Board of Education (2012), pp.1-4</ref>
On the other hand, during the {{ill|Jōmon transgression|ja|縄文海進}}, the sea reached the foothills of {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}}. Subsequently, as the sea receded, sandbars formed along the {{ill|Kano River|ja|狩野川}}’s estuary, creating a water body between the Ashitaka foothills and the sandbars. This became the prototype for {{ill|Ukishima Marsh|ja|浮島沼}}. Over time, this water body transitioned from a brackish lagoon to a marshland and then to a wetland. During the construction of {{ill|Takaozan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}}, boats could navigate to within 2–3 kilometers southwest of the kofun.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), p.1; Numazu City Cultural Heritage Center (2016), p.3</ref>
Finally, from the very end of the {{ill|Yayoi period|ja|弥生時代}} to the early {{ill|Kofun period|ja|古墳時代}}, new scoria layers were deposited on the Ashitaka foothills, including the area around {{ill|Takaozan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}}. The rear mound of {{ill|Takaozan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}} was constructed directly atop these new scoria layers.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), pp.4, 15</ref>
== location and Environment of the Kofun == [[File:Ashitaka Volcano Relief Map, SRTM-1 and Takaozan kofun.jpg|thumb|300px|Relief map of Mount Ashitaka and surrounding areas. The red circle marks Takaozan Kofun's location, while the southeast area shaded white represents the former Ukishima Marsh.]] Takaozan Kofun is situated at the terminus of a ridge

[[Takaosan Kofun]]{{Expand Japanese}} {{Otheruses||Kofun on Mount Takao in Kashiwara City, Osaka Prefecture (Takaozan Site)|Takaozan (Osaka Prefecture)}} {{{{Infobox ancient site |name = Takaozan Kofun |image = [[File:Takaosan-kofun (Numazu) zenkei.JPG|280px]]Full view of the tumulus (foreground left: front section, background right: rear section)(as of June 2015) |location = [[Higashikumando]], [[Numazu City]], [[Shizuoka Prefecture]] |latitude = 35|latitude_min = 7|latitude_sec = 22.73 |longitude =138|longitude_min = 51|longitude_sec = 40.22 |ISO = JP-22 |shape = [[Zenpō-kōhō-fun]] |dimensions = Tumulus length: 62mHeight: 4.7m (estimated at approximately 5m) |burial_facility = [[Wooden coffin]] direct burial |construction_date = Around the year [[250]] |buried_person = |grave_goods = Bronze mirror (animal belt mirror of the embossed style from the Shangfang Workshop) 1 piece, magatama 1 piece, spear 1 piece, 32 iron arrowheads, 1 spearhead-plane, and a large amount of earthenware from the tumulus and the surrounding ditch. |cultural_property_designation = [[Historic Site]] designated by the national government ("Takaozan Kofun") |notable_features = |map = Japan Shizuoka |icon = Zenpō-kōhō-fun - South }} {{osm box|n|4735442868}}
'''Takaozan Kofun''' (Takaozan burial mound) is a [[kofun]] located in [[Higashikumando]] ("East Kumando"), [[Numazu City]], [[Shizuoka Prefecture]]. It has the form of a [[Zenpō-kōhō-fun]] (keyhole-shaped mound with a rectangular rear and trapezoidal front)Numazu City Board of Education (2012) summary report. It has been designated as a [[Historic Site]] by the national government.[https://www.bunka.go.jp/koho_hodo_oshirase/hodohappyo/94070501.html Cultural Council's Recommendation (Designation of Historic Sites, Places of Scenic Beauty, and Natural Monuments)] (Agency for Cultural Affairs press release, June 24, 2024).Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology, Notification No. 142, October 11, 2024.
The Numazu City Board of Education estimates its construction to have been around the year [[250]], during the early [[Kofun period]] (the period of the [[Yamatai Kingdom]]), making it one of the oldest and largest kofun in Eastern Japan from the early appearance of such burial mounds.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/profile/bunkazai/kofun/takaosan.htm Numazu City, 2024, "Takaozan Kofun"] Accessed October 20, 2024. The [[Japanese Archaeological Association]] has evaluated it as an extremely important site for understanding the process of forming the early statehood marked by the kofun culture.[http://archaeology.jp/maibun/nikokyo2015-12.htm Japanese Archaeological Association, 2015, "Statement by the President Calling for Preservation of the Takaozan Kofun in Numazu City, Shizuoka Prefecture"] Accessed July 8, 2017.
Additionally, the site lies in the path of the planned construction of the urban arterial road (Numazu South Isshiki Line), which Numazu City considers a critical route for the urban structure.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/takaosan/jyoukyou.htm Numazu City, "Status of Urban Arterial Road Construction for Numazu South Isshiki Line"] Accessed July 8, 2017. Consequently, debates regarding the coexistence of road construction and kofun preservation have taken place, with various measures being examined to achieve both.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/g-shigiki/g-sigiki/dayori/h27/pdf/207-10.pdf Numazu City, 2015, "Submission of a Petition Regarding the Continuation of the Takaozan Kofun" (PDF file)] Accessed July 8, 2017. [https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/takaosan/index.htm Numazu City, 2017, "Preservation of the Takaozan Kofun and Road Development"] Accessed July 8, 2017.

Additionally, the site lies in the path of the planned construction of the urban arterial road (Numazu South Isshiki Line), which Numazu City considers a critical route for the urban structure.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/takaosan/jyoukyou.htm Numazu City, "Status of Urban Arterial Road Construction for Numazu South Isshiki Line"] Accessed July 8, 2017. Consequently, debates regarding the coexistence of road construction and kofun preservation have taken place, with various measures being examined to achieve both.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/g-shigiki/g-sigiki/dayori/h27/pdf/207-10.pdf Numazu City, 2015, "Submission of a Petition Regarding the Continuation of the Takaozan Kofun" (PDF file)] Accessed July 8, 2017. [https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/takaosan/index.htm Numazu City, 2017, "Preservation of the Takaozan Kofun and Road Development"] Accessed July 8, 2017.
== Location and Environment of the Burial Mound == [[File:Ashitaka Volcano Relief Map, SRTM-1 and Takkaosan kofun.jpg|thumb|300px|Map of {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}} and its surroundings. The red circle indicates the location of Takaozan Kofun. The lowland area to the southeast, marked in white, corresponds to the former {{ill|Ukishima Marsh|ja|浮島沼}}.]] The {{ill|Takaozan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}} is located at the southernmost ridge extending from {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}}. The elevation at the site of the kofun is approximately 20 meters. While situated on a ridge, it cannot be regarded as a burial mound constructed on elevated terrain.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2012), p.1; Sato (2013a), p.11</ref>
{{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}} is believed to have begun activity around 400,000 years ago. From about 170,000 years ago, it actively emitted {{ill|andesite|ja|安山岩}} and {{ill|dacite|ja|デイサイト}} lava flows towards its southeastern flank, forming the gentle hills now seen in the areas of modern-day {{ill|Numazu|ja|沼津市}} City and {{ill|Nagaizumi|ja|長泉町}} Town. {{ill|Takaozan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}} was constructed at the edge of these hills, shaped by volcanic activity that began roughly 170,000 years ago.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), pp.36; Numazu City Board of Education (2012), pp.1-4</ref>
The volcanic activity of {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}} ended about 100,000 years ago. Subsequently, the nearby {{ill|Ancient Mount Fuji|ja|古富士火山}} became active, depositing large amounts of volcanic ash on the lower slopes of Ashitaka. This ash formed thick {{ill|loam|ja|ローム層}} layers. During the latter period of Ancient Mount Fuji’s activity, an upper loam layer developed, characterized by alternating {{ill|scoria|ja|スコリア}} layers and black bands of humus soil. During this time, volcanic deposits from the {{ill|Aira Caldera|ja|姶良カルデラ}}'s massive eruption, about 25,000 years ago, also accumulated in the Ashitaka foothills, mixing with deposits from Ancient Mount Fuji to create a stratum known as pseudo-loam.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), pp.37, 67; Numazu City Board of Education (2012), p.4</ref>
After Ancient Mount Fuji became dormant, the activity of the {{ill|New Fuji Volcano|ja|新期富士火山}} began around 11,000 years ago. Initially, the volcanic activity was dominated by large lava flows, which were obstructed by {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}} and did not reach the area around {{ill|Takaozan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}}. As a result, black soil layers developed in the Ashitaka foothills, forming the uppermost part of the loam layers. By the late {{ill|Jōmon period|ja|縄文時代}}, approximately 3,200 years ago, significant pumice eruptions occurred at {{ill|Kawago-daira|ja|カワゴ平}}, part of the {{ill|Izu East Volcano Group|ja|伊豆東部火山群}}. However, these eruptions did not leave significant layers in the Ashitaka region. During the same period, large-scale {{ill|mountain collapses|ja|山体崩壊}} occurred on the eastern slopes of Mount Fuji, creating massive debris flows that accumulated in the {{ill|Kise River|ja|黄瀬川}} basin. These events formed the {{ill|Kise River alluvial fan|ja|黄瀬川扇状地}}, transforming the eastern parts of modern-day {{ill|Numazu|ja|沼津市}} City from wetlands into dry land by the start of the {{ill|Yayoi period|ja|弥生時代}}.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), p.38; Numazu City Board of Education (2012), pp.1-4</ref>
On the other hand, during the {{ill|Jōmon transgression|ja|縄文海進}}, the sea reached the foothills of {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}}. Subsequently, as the sea receded, sandbars formed along the {{ill|Kano River|ja|狩野川}}’s estuary, creating a water body between the Ashitaka foothills and the sandbars. This became the prototype for {{ill|Ukishima Marsh|ja|浮島沼}}. Over time, this water body transitioned from a brackish lagoon to a marshland and then to a wetland. During the construction of {{ill|Takaozan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}}, boats could navigate to within 2–3 kilometers southwest of the kofun.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), p.1; Numazu City Cultural Heritage Center (2016), p.3</ref>
Finally, from the very end of the {{ill|Yayoi period|ja|弥生時代}} to the early {{ill|Kofun period|ja|古墳時代}}, new scoria layers were deposited on the Ashitaka foothills, including the area around {{ill|Takaozan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}}. The rear mound of {{ill|Takaozan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}} was constructed directly atop these new scoria layers.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), pp.4, 15</ref>

'''Takaozan Kofun''' (Takaozan burial mound) is a [[kofun]] located in [[Higashikumando]] ("East Kumando"), [[Numazu City]], [[Shizuoka Prefecture]]. It has the form of a [[Zenpō-kōhō-fun]] (keyhole-shaped mound with a rectangular rear and trapezoidal front)Numazu City Board of Education (2012) summary report. It has been designated as a [[Historic Site]] by the national government.[https://www.bunka.go.jp/koho_hodo_oshirase/hodohappyo/94070501.html Cultural Council's Recommendation (Designation of Historic Sites, Places of Scenic Beauty, and Natural Monuments)] (Agency for Cultural Affairs press release, June 24, 2024).Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology, Notification No. 142, October 11, 2024.
The Numazu City Board of Education estimates its construction to have been around the year [[250]], during the early [[Kofun period]] (the period of the [[Yamatai Kingdom]]), making it one of the oldest and largest kofun in Eastern Japan from the early appearance of such burial mounds.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/profile/bunkazai/kofun/takaosan.htm Numazu City, 2024, "Takaozan Kofun"] Accessed October 20, 2024. The [[Japanese Archaeological Association]] has evaluated it as an extremely important site for understanding the process of forming the early statehood marked by the kofun culture.[http://archaeology.jp/maibun/nikokyo2015-12.htm Japanese Archaeological Association, 2015, "Statement by the President Calling for Preservation of the Takaozan Kofun in Numazu City, Shizuoka Prefecture"] Accessed July 8, 2017.
Additionally, the site lies in the path of the planned construction of the urban arterial road (Numazu South Isshiki Line), which Numazu City considers a critical route for the urban structure.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/takaosan/jyoukyou.htm Numazu City, "Status of Urban Arterial Road Construction for Numazu South Isshiki Line"] Accessed July 8, 2017. Consequently, debates regarding the coexistence of road construction and kofun preservation have taken place, with various measures being examined to achieve both.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/g-shigiki/g-sigiki/dayori/h27/pdf/207-10.pdf Numazu City, 2015, "Submission of a Petition Regarding the Continuation of the Takaozan Kofun" (PDF file)] Accessed July 8, 2017. [https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/takaosan/index.htm Numazu City, 2017, "Preservation of the Takaozan Kofun and Road Development"] Accessed July 8, 2017.

The Numazu City Board of Education estimates its construction to have been around the year [[250]], during the early [[Kofun period]] (the period of the [[Yamatai Kingdom]]), making it one of the oldest and largest kofun in Eastern Japan from the early appearance of such burial mounds.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/profile/bunkazai/kofun/takaosan.htm Numazu City, 2024, "Takaozan Kofun"] Accessed October 20, 2024. The [[Japanese Archaeological Association]] has evaluated it as an extremely important site for understanding the process of forming the early statehood marked by the kofun culture.[http://archaeology.jp/maibun/nikokyo2015-12.htm Japanese Archaeological Association, 2015, "Statement by the President Calling for Preservation of the Takaozan Kofun in Numazu City, Shizuoka Prefecture"] Accessed July 8, 2017.
Additionally, the site lies in the path of the planned construction of the urban arterial road (Numazu South Isshiki Line), which Numazu City considers a critical route for the urban structure.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/takaosan/jyoukyou.htm Numazu City, "Status of Urban Arterial Road Construction for Numazu South Isshiki Line"] Accessed July 8, 2017. Consequently, debates regarding the coexistence of road construction and kofun preservation have taken place, with various measures being examined to achieve both.[https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/g-shigiki/g-sigiki/dayori/h27/pdf/207-10.pdf Numazu City, 2015, "Submission of a Petition Regarding the Continuation of the Takaozan Kofun" (PDF file)] Accessed July 8, 2017. [https://www.city.numazu.shizuoka.jp/shisei/takaosan/index.htm Numazu City, 2017, "Preservation of the Takaozan Kofun and Road Development"] Accessed July 8, 2017.
== Location and Environment of the Burial Mound == [[File:Ashitaka Volcano Relief Map, SRTM-1 and Takkaosan kofun.jpg|thumb|300px|Map of {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}} and its surroundings. The red circle indicates the location of Takaozan Kofun. The lowland area to the southeast, marked in white, corresponds to the former {{ill|Ukishima Marsh|ja|浮島沼}}.]] The {{ill|Takaozan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}} is located at the southernmost ridge extending from {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}}. The elevation at the site of the kofun is approximately 20 meters. While situated on a ridge, it cannot be regarded as a burial mound constructed on elevated terrain.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2012), p.1; Sato (2013a), p.11</ref>
{{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}} is believed to have begun activity around 400,000 years ago. From about 170,000 years ago, it actively emitted {{ill|andesite|ja|安山岩}} and {{ill|dacite|ja|デイサイト}} lava flows towards its southeastern flank, forming the gentle hills now seen in the areas of modern-day {{ill|Numazu|ja|沼津市}} City and {{ill|Nagaizumi|ja|長泉町}} Town. {{ill|Takaozan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}} was constructed at the edge of these hills, shaped by volcanic activity that began roughly 170,000 years ago.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), pp.36; Numazu City Board of Education (2012), pp.1-4</ref>
The volcanic activity of {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}} ended about 100,000 years ago. Subsequently, the nearby {{ill|Ancient Mount Fuji|ja|古富士火山}} became active, depositing large amounts of volcanic ash on the lower slopes of Ashitaka. This ash formed thick {{ill|loam|ja|ローム層}} layers. During the latter period of Ancient Mount Fuji’s activity, an upper loam layer developed, characterized by alternating {{ill|scoria|ja|スコリア}} layers and black bands of humus soil. During this time, volcanic deposits from the {{ill|Aira Caldera|ja|姶良カルデラ}}'s massive eruption, about 25,000 years ago, also accumulated in the Ashitaka foothills, mixing with deposits from Ancient Mount Fuji to create a stratum known as pseudo-loam.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), pp.37, 67; Numazu City Board of Education (2012), p.4</ref>
After Ancient Mount Fuji became dormant, the activity of the {{ill|New Fuji Volcano|ja|新期富士火山}} began around 11,000 years ago. Initially, the volcanic activity was dominated by large lava flows, which were obstructed by {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}} and did not reach the area around {{ill|Takaozan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}}. As a result, black soil layers developed in the Ashitaka foothills, forming the uppermost part of the loam layers. By the late {{ill|Jōmon period|ja|縄文時代}}, approximately 3,200 years ago, significant pumice eruptions occurred at {{ill|Kawago-daira|ja|カワゴ平}}, part of the {{ill|Izu East Volcano Group|ja|伊豆東部火山群}}. However, these eruptions did not leave significant layers in the Ashitaka region. During the same period, large-scale {{ill|mountain collapses|ja|山体崩壊}} occurred on the eastern slopes of Mount Fuji, creating massive debris flows that accumulated in the {{ill|Kise River|ja|黄瀬川}} basin. These events formed the {{ill|Kise River alluvial fan|ja|黄瀬川扇状地}}, transforming the eastern parts of modern-day {{ill|Numazu|ja|沼津市}} City from wetlands into dry land by the start of the {{ill|Yayoi period|ja|弥生時代}}.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), p.38; Numazu City Board of Education (2012), pp.1-4</ref>
On the other hand, during the {{ill|Jōmon transgression|ja|縄文海進}}, the sea reached the foothills of {{ill|Ashitaka Volcano|ja|愛鷹山}}. Subsequently, as the sea receded, sandbars formed along the {{ill|Kano River|ja|狩野川}}’s estuary, creating a water body between the Ashitaka foothills and the sandbars. This became the prototype for {{ill|Ukishima Marsh|ja|浮島沼}}. Over time, this water body transitioned from a brackish lagoon to a marshland and then to a wetland. During the construction of {{ill|Takaozan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}}, boats could navigate to within 2–3 kilometers southwest of the kofun.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), p.1; Numazu City Cultural Heritage Center (2016), p.3</ref>
Finally, from the very end of the {{ill|Yayoi period|ja|弥生時代}} to the early {{ill|Kofun period|ja|古墳時代}}, new scoria layers were deposited on the Ashitaka foothills, including the area around {{ill|Takaozan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}}. The rear mound of {{ill|Takaozan Kofun|ja|高尾山古墳}} was constructed directly atop these new scoria layers.<ref>Numazu City Board of Education (2005), pp.4, 15</ref>
== location and Environment of the Kofun == [[File:Ashitaka Volcano Relief Map, SRTM-1 and Takaozan kofun.jpg|thumb|300px|Relief map of Mount Ashitaka and surrounding areas. The red circle marks Takaozan Kofun's location, while the southeast area shaded white represents the former Ukishima Marsh.]] Takaozan Kofun is situated at the terminus of a ridge
